paper_title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.

Thus, we define Implicit Intent as communicative goal that is not directly and fully stated in literal verbal content, but can be inferred from verbal cues, observable nonverbal behavior, and available context. For interactive digital humans, understanding such intent must be reflected in generated language, vocal expression, and visible behavior. Whether digital human recognizes users unstated needs and addresses them appropriately is therefore an important criterion for evaluating its interactive quality. In Case of Figure 1, Tavus focuses on whether Im dead is joke and misses the speakers distress about quitting his job. In Case II, Vidu responds playfully to another speakers account of performing for her parents guests, overlooking the sense of obligation in her words had to do play. Appendix (Case and Case E) shows how five digital human systems responded to these two user clips. Existing research provides evaluation foundations for both intent understanding and response generation. MIntRec2.0 assesses intent recognition through multimodal classification (Zhang et al., 2024), while VAGUE uses images to disambiguate what speaker is asking someone to do (Nam et al., 2025). For subset of its clips, GesBench asks annotators what the speaker intends, how the listener might respond, and what led them to those judgments (Li et al., 2026). AvaMERG evaluates empathy in textual replies and the consistency of content and style across text, speech, and avatar video (Zhang et al., 2025a). VidChatBench assesses dialogue coherence and audiovisual generation quality (Zhang et al., 2025c), while LiveTalk evaluates response content, nonverbal engagement, and consistency across turns (Chern et al., 2025). However, these benchmarks do not systematically evaluate whether generated digital human responses fulfill the implicit communicative intent conveyed by users 2 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview Figure 2. Evaluation pipeline of UUBench. (a) user describes dance as lifeline, and an avatar responds. (b) The speakers words, soft voice, lowered gaze, and upturned palms provide evidence that she seeks support and understanding. (c) Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV assesses audiovisual response quality (Q) and how well the response addresses the needs conveyed by each applicable primitive. The latter scores are reported by dimension (xk) and combined within each response using evidence-based weights to obtain the system score after averaging across clips. multimodal cues. reply can sound natural and stay on topic while overlooking the speakers need for acknowledgment. Evaluating such intent fulfillment requires explicitly linking the evidence supporting the inferred intent to the digital humans response. To address this gap, we introduce UUBench, benchmark for evaluating how well digital humans respond to users implicit communicative intentions. Implicit intent is not directly observable, and inferring it from an interaction involves subjective judgment. single rating of intent fulfillment can obscure which aspects of the users need reply addresses. We therefore introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds this assessment in observable auditory and visual cues. As shown in Figure 2, the speaker describes how dance sustained her. The annotated evidence links her words, soft voice, and lowered gaze to an inferred need for support and understanding. We score the reply separately for each applicable primitive dimension based on how well it addresses the need conveyed by the corresponding cues. We then combine these scores using weights derived from the relevance of each primitives la3 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview bels to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring assesses the quality of the reply itself by rating its naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness under audio, visual, and joint audiovisual observation. To ground both types of scores in observable evidence, our FactGrounded Scoring JEV module uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations to evaluate one primitive dimension or quality criterion at time. We selected 28,548 candidate user clips from four video sources TalkVerse (Wang et al., 2025), TalkCuts (Chen et al., 2025a), TalkVid (Chen et al., 2025b), and SpeakerVid-5M (Zhang et al., 2025c). Human reviewers then selected 216 high-quality clips from this pool for evaluation. For each selected clip, annotators labeled the speakers intent and the auditory and visual primitives, then recorded the words and observable behaviors that supported their interpretation. We evaluated five closed-source and four open-source digital human systems on these same 216 inputs. All nine systems received positive overall audiovisual quality scores (Q = 1.012.03), yet each had negative mean score on every visual primitive dimension  (Table 4)  . These results suggest shared difficulty among the evaluated systems in addressing communicative needs conveyed through facial behavior, gaze, head movements, and gestures. Our main contributions are: 1. benchmark for implicit intent fulfillment. We introduce UUBench to evaluate whether digital human responses address users implicit communicative intent. From pool of 28,548 user clips, we selected 216 for evaluation. For each selected clip, annotators identified the speakers intent, labeled the auditory and visual primitives, and recorded the words and behaviors supporting their interpretation. 2. Scoring response quality and intent fulfillment. We introduce two complementary scoring perspectives (Figure 2): Process-Oriented Scoring assesses how well the reply addresses the need conveyed by each applicable primitive. Outcome-Oriented Scoring measures audiovisual response quality (Q). Our Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module grounds both assessments in structured audio-visual observations. We report primitive-level scores and aggregate them using evidence-based weights within each reply, then average across clips to obtain the system-level intent-fulfillment score (S). 3. Comparative evaluation of responses to implicit intent. We evaluated five closed-source and four open-source digital human systems with UUBench. All nine achieve positive overall audiovisual quality scores, yet each receives negative mean intent-fulfillment scores across all four visual primitive dimensions: facial behavior, gaze, head movements, and gestures  (Table 4)  . sections.title: 2.1 Multimodal Intent Recognition and Pragmatic Understanding
sections.content: Multimodal intent benchmarks examine how language, nonverbal behavior, and context inform communicative interpretation. MIntRec provides utterancelevel intent classification (Zhang et al., 2022), while MIntRec2.0 extends this setting to multi-party conversations and out-of-scope detection (Zhang et al., 2024). VAGUE pairs an ambiguous expression with an image and asks what action the speaker is requesting (Nam et al., 2025). READI tests whether models can use an image to infer speakers directive intent across three levels of indirectness in the utterance (Kim et al., 2026). GesBench examines how interpretations change as an utterance unfolds. For 590 of its 6,208 clips, annotators describe the speakers intent, suggest how listener might respond, and explain their judgments (Li et al., 2026). Table 1 summarizes the references these tasks provide. Predicting what listener might do and evaluating how well an actual reply addresses the speakers need are distinct tasks.

sections.title: 2.2 Interactive Digital Human Generation
sections.content: Interactive digital human generation combines conversational behavior with INFP uses both participants audio to animate an audiovisual synthesis. 5 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview avatars head and face as it speaks and listens (Zhu et al., 2025), while Avatar Forcing conditions causal generation on user audio and motion together with avatar speech to support real-time reactions (Ki et al., 2026). Sustained interaction also requires temporal consistency and behavioral control. SoulX-LiveAct enables hour-scale, real-time animation with bounded historical memory and controllable expressions and actions (Zhen et al., 2026). At the conversational-system level, LiveTalk connects an audio language model with streaming video generation for multi-turn interaction (Chern et al., 2025), while InteractiveAvatar uses transcribed user speech and the avatars current state to plan spoken reply and accompanying actions (Song et al., 2026). These developments make coordinated speech and visible feedback central to digital human interaction. Evaluating such systems therefore requires assessing both the quality of audiovisual realization and whether the generated behavior appropriately responds to the users communicative goal.

sections.title: 2.3 Evaluation of Digital Human Responses
sections.content: Existing evaluations address several aspects of this problem. THEval measures talking-head quality, naturalness, and synchronization (Quignon et al., 2025). ViCo evaluates responsive listening behavior using paired speaker listener recordings (Zhou et al., 2022); MARS, introduced for REACT 2025, supports multiple acceptable facial reactions and evaluates appropriateness, diversity, synchrony, and realism (Song et al., 2025). AvaMERG annotates emotion causes and response goals to support empathetic reasoning. Its human evaluation rates empathy in textual replies and assesses the consistency of content and style across text, speech, and avatar video (Zhang et al., 2025a). VidChatBench evaluates dialogue coherence alongside visual quality, identity preservation, audiovisual synchronization, and the alignment of facial expressions in generated and reference videos (Zhang et al., 2025c). LiveTalk evaluates the semantic relevance of replies, nonverbal engagement, and visual and behavioral consistency across turns (Chern et al., 2025). UUBench links each annotated intent to observable cues in the users clip. For each applicable auditory or visual primitive, it scores how well the generated reply addresses the need those cues convey. For example, user describing friends move abroad as great opportunity for her may speak at lower pitch and volume, shift their gaze downward, turn down the corners of their mouth, and bow their head. digital human should interpret these cues in context and recognize that the user may be seeking acknowledgment of their reluctance to part and disappointment about the separation. sections.title: 3.3 Annotating Intent, Primitives, and Supporting Evidence
sections.content: For each of the 216 evaluation clips, human annotators identified the speakers communicative intent (I) and labeled the applicable auditory and visual primitives (P ). Table 2 groups the cues into four auditory and four visual dimensions. For example, the prosody dimension captures pauses and changes in pitch, while the speaker-emotion dimension describes the affect or stance conveyed by the voice. Annotators interpreted the speakers words alongside the vocal and visual cues they identified in the clip. After labeling the intent and primitives, they documented the supporting evidence (E). In the evidence annotation, annotators identified relevant words, vocal cues, or visible behaviors in the clip and explained how these supported their interpretation of the speakers intent. For clip j, the primitive labels determine the set of dimensions Kj used to evaluate every systems reply to that clip. On each dimension, we assess how well the reply addresses the need conveyed by the users cues. In Figure 2, for example, the speakers soft voice and lowered gaze give context to her account of how dance sustained her. digital human can address her implied need for understanding by acknowledging in words what dance has meant to her. 8 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview Figure 4. Examples of user clips and digital human responses. Each case presents sampled frames and transcripts from the user and the responding system. The examples illustrate acknowledgment of personal experience (Case 1), playful reply to recollection of being expected to perform (Case 2), and follow-up question prompted by figurative expression (Case 3). Audio delivery and temporal coordination cannot be fully assessed from static frames and transcripts alone.

sections.title: 3.4 Perception and Evidence Preparation
sections.content: The annotated intent Ij records the annotators interpretation of the speakers goal. Our Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module uses timestamped observations of the user clip and the avatars response to assign the scores in Figure 2(c). For each outcome-oriented score qj,m,c, Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) retains the full user context and rates one quality criterion using the audio, visual, or combined audiovisual observations of the response. For each processoriented score xjk, Jev uses the full audiovisual observations of both participants and the users labels for primitive to judge how well the reply addresses the need conveyed by those cues (Figure 5). We use the relevance of those labels to the annotators supporting evidence Ej to weight the resulting primitive scores (Section 3.6). 9 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview Figure 5. The Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module. Visual and auditory observers describe the user clip and avatar reply. For each quality judgment (q), Jev receives the full user observations, reply fields selected for the Audio, Visual, or Omni view, all eight source primitive dimensions, and any measurements assigned to that criterion. For primitive judgment (xjk), Jev receives the full audiovisual observations and only the target dimensions labels. The seven rubric anchors span 3 to +3. Visual descriptions use silent frames sampled at target rate of 6 FPS, with native timestamps retained. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (Qwen Team, 2026) generates visual descriptions for all user clips and for responses from all nine systems. Transcription and alignment use Qwen3-ASR-1.7B and Qwen3ForcedAligner-0.6B (Shi et al., 2026). Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct (Xu et al., 2025) describes audible delivery and other sounds from the audio track alone. These descriptions, aligned utterances, and time-localized visual observations form the records that Jev scores. This observation stage preserves the original primitive labels and applicability masks. Appendix B.2 provides the prompts used to describe the visual and auditory content of the user clips and avatar replies. Technical measurements supplement these descriptions: SyncNet supplies lip-synchronization evidence, Q-Align supplies image quality, and framebased measures characterize motion smoothness and temporal stability (Chung and Zisserman, 2016; Wu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). Each measurement is supplied only to relevant outcome criteria. Primitive scoring receives audiovisual descriptions without these measurements, and source weights are withheld from all Jev requests.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluated nine digital human systems on the same 216 user clips. The five closed-source systems were Emma (Nuance Labs, 2026), Tavus (n.d.), Vidu (n.d.), D-ID (n.d.), and bitHuman (n.d.). The four open-source systems were CyberVerse (Lynpoint, n.d.) with SoulX-LiveAct (Zhen et al., 2026), OpenAvatarChat (Cheng et al., 2025) with LiteAvatar (Zhuang et al., 2022), Open-LLM-VTuber (n.d.) with Live2D (Live2D Inc., n.d.), and EmpaAva (Yang et al., 2026) with GaussianAvatars (Qian et al., 2024) and DEEPTalk (Kim et al., 2025). We used the same response-generation prompt for all nine systems (Appendix B.1) and scored all replies using the protocol in Section 3.

sections.title: 4.2 Overall Results
sections.content: All nine systems received positive overall audiovisual quality scores (Q = 1.01 to 2.03). sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce UUBench to evaluate how well digital humans respond to what users leave unsaid. From collection of 28,548 user clips, we curated 216 evaluation clips and annotated each speakers intent, the auditory and visual primitives present in the clip, and the evidence linking those cues to the intent. These annotations make it possible to ask which aspects of an inferred need reply addresses. Our Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module uses structured observations of the user and the digital human for both assessments. Outcome-oriented scoring evaluates the audiovisual quality of the reply. Process-oriented scoring evaluates how well the reply addresses the need conveyed by each applicable primitive, then combines the scores using weights derived from the annotated evidence. Evaluating five closed-source and four open-source systems on the same clips revealed consistent gap between audiovisual quality and responsiveness to visual cues. All nine systems earned positive overall audiovisual quality scores, yet each had negative mean scores for responding to needs conveyed by facial behavior, gaze, head movements, and gestures  (Table 4)  . digital human may produce natural facial expression yet give reply that overlooks what the users own expression conveys. By scoring how reply addresses the needs supported by specific cues, UUBench identifies which aspects of the users intent the reply may have missed. This allows future eval17 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview uations to test whether improvements in how digital humans look and sound are accompanied by better responses to what users leave unsaid.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The current evaluation set comprises 216 user clips, with limited scale and coverage of communicative intents, interaction contexts, and multimodal cues. Some cues are applicable to relatively few clips, limiting detailed comparisons across contexts and cue combinations. The reported results therefore characterize the evaluated systems on the current dataset; larger-scale evaluations are needed to assess whether these findings generalize to broader interaction settings. The automated judge Jev and the evidence-weighting mechanism have not yet been systematically validated against independent human ratings. Although the framework organizes scoring around concrete audiovisual cues, agreement with human judgments at the dimension level and in overall intent fulfillment remains to be quantified. Whether evidence weighting better reflects human judgments of responses than alternative aggregation schemes also requires validation. The current study also lacks systematic ablations that isolate the contributions of different observation types and the evidence-weighting mechanism. While we evaluate nine digital human systems, further tests across different data sources and additional systems are needed to assess the stability of the scoring framework and establish its scope of applicability. sections.title: Future Plans
sections.content: This preview release establishes an initial evaluation framework for understanding and responding to implicit communicative intent. We plan to develop UUBench further along five directions. Scaling toward UUBench 1.0. We plan to expand the evaluation set beyond the current 216 clips, increasing coverage of communicative intents, interaction contexts, and auditory and visual cues. We also plan to evaluate additional open-source and closed-source digital human systems. We used the same response-generation model, Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct (Xu et al., 2025), across the four open-source systems to control for differences in how replies were generated. We plan to compare additional response-generation models using the same user clips and avatar renderer to assess how model choice affects responses to implicit intent. Human validation, ablations, and generalization. We plan to recruit independent raters to assess the audiovisual quality and intent fulfillment of responses, report inter-rater agreement and agreement between human and 18 inSIght Labs UUBench Preview automated ratings, and analyze cases of disagreement. To validate evidence weighting, we will hold dimension-level scores fixed and compare evidenceweighted aggregation with equal weighting over applicable dimensions, assessing how well each scheme matches independent human judgments of overall intent fulfillment. We will also conduct ablations that remove different types of observational information to isolate their contributions to the corresponding scoring tasks. We will repeat these validations across different data sources and additional digital human systems to assess whether agreement with human judgments remains stable. Supplementary materials will document the validation results, qualitative examples, and visualizations of system behavior. Training intent-aware digital humans. Beyond evaluation, we aim to explore how intent annotations, supporting evidence, and primitive-level feedback can support model training. central research question is how digital humans can translate multimodal intent understanding into responses that appropriately address users communicative needs through language, vocal expression, and visible behavior. Extending to multi-turn interaction. The current evaluation focuses on individual responses to user clips. Future benchmarks will extend this setting to multi-turn conversations, where intent may emerge gradually, change over time, or require clarification. We aim to examine whether digital humans track these developments, use conversational history, and repair misunderstandings across turns. We also plan to investigate how response timing and turntaking interact with intent fulfillment in full-duplex settings. Releasing evaluation resources. We plan to progressively release evaluation protocols, scoring rubrics, and supporting code to facilitate reproducible comparisons. Subject to source-data permissions and privacy considerations, we also aim to provide annotations and data preparation instructions. The release scope and schedule will be documented as the benchmark develops.
